name: Chapter 9: Mechanical Properties of Fluids
description: Pressure, Pascal’s law, hydraulics, continuity, Bernoulli’s principle, Torricelli, lift, viscosity, Stokes’ law, surface tension, capillarity

cards.term: What makes a substance a fluid?
cards.definition: It can flow: liquids and gases

cards.term: Key mechanical difference between fluids and solids?
cards.definition: Fluids offer very little resistance to shear stress (about a million times less than solids); they have no shape of their own

cards.term: Liquid vs gas: volume?
cards.definition: A liquid has a fixed volume and a free surface; a gas fills its container and is highly compressible

cards.term: Why does a needle pierce the skin but a spoon does not, for the same force?
cards.definition: Smaller area → larger pressure (force per unit area)

cards.term: Why is the force of a fluid at rest always normal to a surface?
cards.definition: A parallel component would make the fluid flow (third law); a fluid at rest cannot

cards.term: Define pressure; scalar or vector?
cards.definition: \[P = \lim_{\Delta A \to 0}\dfrac{\Delta F}{\Delta A}\](normal force per area): a scalar; unit pascal, [M L⁻¹ T⁻²]

cards.term: 1 atm, 1 bar, 1 torr in Pa?
cards.definition: 1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa 1 torr = 1 mm Hg = 133 Pa

cards.term: Relative density; density of water at 4 °C?
cards.definition: Density ÷ density of water at 4 °C (dimensionless). Water: 1.0 × 10³ kg m⁻³

cards.term: Example 9.1: two femurs (10 cm² each) carry 40 kg. Average pressure?
cards.definition: 400 N / 20 × 10⁻⁴ m² = 2 × 10⁵ Pa

cards.term: Exercise 9.5: a 50 kg girl balances on one circular heel of diameter 1.0 cm. Pressure?
cards.definition: 6.2 × 10⁶ Pa

cards.text: Pascal’s law: in a fluid at rest, pressure is the {{c1::same in all directions}} and the same at all points at the {{c2::same height}}.

cards.term: How is Pascal’s law proved with a small prism?
cards.definition: Balance forces on a tiny right-angled prism: Fb sin θ = Fc, Fb cos θ = Fa with Ab sin θ = Ac, Ab cos θ = Aa → Pa = Pb = Pc

cards.term: Why must pressure be equal at points on the same horizontal level?
cards.definition: Otherwise a horizontal fluid bar would have a net force and flow

cards.term: Pressure difference between two points h apart vertically?
Pressure at depth h in a liquid open to the air?
cards.definition: \[P = P_a + \rho g h\]P − Pₐ is the gauge pressure

cards.term: What is the hydrostatic paradox?
cards.definition: Vessels of different shapes joined at the bottom fill to the same height: pressure depends only on depth, not on shape or amount of liquid

cards.term: Example 9.2: pressure on a swimmer 10 m below a lake surface?
cards.definition: 2.01 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 2 atm (a 100 % increase)

cards.term: Example 9.4: at 1000 m in the sea (ρ = 1.03 × 10³): absolute and gauge pressure; force on a 20 cm × 20 cm submarine window?
cards.definition: ≈ 104 atm and ≈ 103 atm; F = gauge pressure × 0.04 m² = 4.12 × 10⁵ N

cards.term: Exercise 9.1(a): why is blood pressure greater at the feet than at the brain?
cards.definition: The blood column above the feet is taller: extra ρgh

cards.term: Exercise 9.7: an off-shore structure can take 10⁹ Pa. Suitable for 3 km of ocean?
cards.definition: Yes: pressure there ≈ 3 × 10⁷ Pa, far less

cards.term: Who invented the mercury barometer, and how does it work?
cards.definition: Torricelli: a mercury-filled tube inverted in mercury; the column height h gives\[P_a = \rho g h\](≈ 76 cm Hg)

cards.term: What does an open-tube manometer measure?
cards.definition: The gauge pressure P − Pₐ = ρgh; oil for small differences, mercury for large ones

cards.term: Example 9.3: if air had constant density 1.29 kg/m³, how high would the atmosphere reach?
cards.definition: ≈ 8 km (in reality density and g fall; the atmosphere extends beyond 100 km)

cards.term: What does a drop of 10 mm or more in a barometer reading signal?
cards.definition: An approaching storm

cards.term: Exercise 9.6: height of a French-wine barometer (ρ = 984 kg/m³)?
cards.definition: ≈ 10.5 m

cards.term: Exercise 9.1(b): why does air pressure halve by 6 km though the atmosphere is > 100 km thick?
cards.definition: Air is compressible: most of it is packed near the ground, so density falls rapidly with height

cards.term: Exercise 9.9: 10.0 cm of water balances 12.5 cm of spirit over mercury. Specific gravity of spirit?
cards.definition: 0.800

cards.term: Pascal’s law, second form?
cards.definition: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished and equally in all directions

cards.term: Force on the big piston of a hydraulic lift?
cards.definition: \[F_2 = F_1\dfrac{A_2}{A_1}\]mechanical advantage A₂/A₁

cards.term: Trap: does a hydraulic lift give free energy?
cards.definition: No: the large piston moves a smaller distance; A₁d₁ = A₂d₂ (same volume), so work in = work out

cards.term: Example 9.5: syringes of diameter 1.0 cm and 3.0 cm; 10 N on the small one, pushed in 6.0 cm. Force and movement of the big one?
cards.definition: 90 N and 0.67 cm

cards.term: Example 9.6: car lift, pistons of radius 5.0 cm and 15 cm, car 1350 kg. Force F₁ and air pressure needed?
cards.definition: ≈ 1.5 × 10³ N and 1.9 × 10⁵ Pa (about 2 atm)

cards.term: Why do hydraulic brakes brake all wheels equally?
cards.definition: The pedal’s pressure is transmitted equally to all four wheel cylinders through the brake oil

cards.term: Exercise 9.8: hydraulic lift for 3000 kg, load piston 425 cm². Maximum pressure on the small piston?
cards.definition: 6.92 × 10⁵ Pa (same pressure everywhere)

cards.term: When is flow steady?
cards.definition: When the velocity of fluid at each point stays constant in time (it may differ from point to point)

cards.term: Define a streamline.
cards.definition: The path of a fluid particle in steady flow; its tangent gives the fluid velocity at each point

cards.term: Why can two streamlines never cross?
cards.definition: At the crossing a particle would have two velocities; the flow would not be steady

cards.term: Equation of continuity?
cards.definition: \[A_1v_1 = A_2v_2\](Av = constant) for an incompressible fluid: conservation of mass

cards.term: What do crowded streamlines mean?
cards.definition: Higher speed (narrow cross-section)

cards.term: Laminar vs turbulent flow?
cards.definition: Laminar: layers slide smoothly, parallel velocities. Turbulent: irregular, eddies, above a critical speed

cards.term: Teacher addition (JEE): Reynolds number and its meaning?
cards.definition: \[R_e = \dfrac{\rho v d}{\eta}\]< ~1000 laminar, > ~2000 turbulent

cards.term: Exercise 9.4(b): why does water gush out fast when you cover most of a tap with your fingers?
cards.definition: Smaller outlet area → larger speed (Av = constant)

cards.term: Exercise 9.16: spray pump tube 8.0 cm², 40 holes of 1.0 mm diameter, flow 1.5 m/min inside. Ejection speed?
cards.definition: 0.64 m/s (continuity)

cards.term: State Bernoulli’s equation.
cards.definition: \[P + \tfrac12\rho v^2 + \rho g h = constant\]along a streamline

cards.term: What does each term of Bernoulli’s equation mean?
cards.definition: P: pressure (work per volume) ½ρv²: KE per unit volume ρgh: PE per unit volume

cards.term: Bernoulli’s equation is an expression of which principle?
cards.definition: Conservation of energy (work-energy theorem applied to a fluid element)

cards.term: Correction: NCERT says the work-energy theorem is in "Chapter 6". Where is it?
cards.definition: Chapter 5 (Work, Energy and Power); left over from the old numbering

cards.term: When Bernoulli’s equation applies
cards.definition: Viscosity: zero (non-viscous fluid); Compressibility: incompressible; Type of flow: steady, streamline (not turbulent)

advancedHtml.backHtml:
9.4 · limits of Bernoulli

Assumption needed?

Viscosityzero (non-viscous fluid)
Compressibilityincompressible
Type of flowsteady, streamline (not turbulent)

cards.term: Bernoulli’s equation for a fluid at rest?
cards.definition: Reduces to\[P_1 - P_2 = \rho g(h_2 - h_1)\]the hydrostatic result

cards.term: Daniel Bernoulli gave the equation in which year?
cards.definition: 1738

cards.term: Flow through a constriction: speed and pressure
cards.definition: Av = constant so v is largest in the narrow part; P + ½ρv² = constant so pressure is lowest there

advancedHtml.backHtml:
Continuity + Bernoulli · venturi

Water flows steadily through a pipe with a narrow section. Where is it fastest, and where is the pressure lowest?

Continuity: Av = constant, so the fluid speeds up in the narrow part.

Bernoulli (same height): P + ½ρv² = constant, so faster flow means lower pressure: the column above the constriction is shortest.

cards.term: Exercise 9.15: which of the two flows through a constriction is wrong?
cards.definition: The one showing higher liquid level (pressure) at the constriction: there v is larger, so P must be lower

cards.term: Exercise 9.11: can Bernoulli’s equation describe water through river rapids?
cards.definition: No: the flow is turbulent, not streamline

cards.term: Exercise 9.12: does it matter if gauge pressure is used in Bernoulli’s equation?
cards.definition: No, unless the atmospheric pressure differs significantly between the two points

cards.term: Torricelli’s law: speed of efflux from a hole h below the surface of an open tank?
cards.definition: \[v = \sqrt{2gh}\]same as free fall from h

cards.term: Speed of efflux from a closed tank at pressure P?
cards.definition: \[v = \sqrt{2gh + \dfrac{2(P - P_a)}{\rho}}\]if P ≫ Pₐ the pressure term dominates (rocket propulsion)

cards.term: Exercise 9.4(d): why does fluid leaving a hole push the vessel backwards?
cards.definition: The out-flowing fluid carries momentum; by the third law the vessel gets an equal backward thrust

cards.term: What is dynamic lift?
cards.definition: Force on a body such as a wing, hydrofoil or spinning ball due to its motion through a fluid

cards.term: Magnus effect: why does a spinning ball swerve?
cards.definition: Spin drags air: relative air speed is larger on one side → lower pressure there → sideways/upward force

cards.term: Why does an aerofoil give lift?
cards.definition: Its shape and tilt crowd streamlines above the wing: faster air, lower pressure above than below

cards.term: Example 9.7: 3.3 × 10⁵ kg aircraft, wing area 500 m², 960 km/h. Pressure difference and speed difference?
cards.definition: ΔP = 6.5 × 10³ Pa; air above needs to be only ≈ 8 % faster

cards.term: Exercise 9.14: wind-tunnel wing, speeds 70 and 63 m/s, area 2.5 m², ρ = 1.3. Lift?
cards.definition: ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²)A ≈ 1.5 × 10³ N

cards.term: Exercise 9.4(a): to keep paper horizontal, blow over it or under it?
cards.definition: Over: faster air above → lower pressure above → paper lifts

cards.term: What is viscosity?
cards.definition: Internal friction between fluid layers moving relative to each other

cards.term: Velocity profile of a liquid between a fixed and a moving plate; in a pipe?
cards.definition: Plates: rises uniformly from 0 to v. Pipe: maximum at the axis, zero at the walls

cards.term: Define the coefficient of viscosity.
cards.definition: \[\eta = \dfrac{F/A}{v/l}\]shear stress ÷ rate of shear strain

cards.term: Solid vs fluid under shear: stress depends on what?
cards.definition: Solid: on shear strain. Fluid: on the rate of shear strain (Exercise 9.3c)

cards.term: SI unit and dimensions of viscosity?
cards.definition: poiseuille (Pl) = N s m⁻² = Pa s; [M L⁻¹ T⁻¹]

cards.term: Effect of temperature on viscosity?
cards.definition: Liquids: η decreases (molecules more mobile). Gases: η increases (more random motion)

cards.term: Example 9.8: 0.10 m² block on a 0.30 mm oil film pulled by 0.010 kg at a steady 0.085 m/s. η?
Exercise 9.4(c): why does needle size control injection flow better than thumb pressure?
cards.definition: Flow through a narrow tube depends very strongly on its radius (∝ r⁴ in viscous flow), much more than on pressure

cards.term: State Stokes’ law.
cards.definition: \[F = 6\pi\eta a v\]viscous drag on a sphere of radius a moving at v

cards.term: Terminal velocity of a sphere in a fluid?
cards.definition: \[v_t = \dfrac{2a^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}\](ρ sphere, σ fluid)

cards.term: Ball in oil: approach to terminal velocity
cards.definition: Speed rises to a constant terminal value when 6πηav + buoyancy = weight; vt = 2a²(ρ−σ)g/9η

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Viscosity · terminal velocity

A small metal ball is dropped into a tall jar of oil. How does its speed change with time?

What force grows with speed?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Viscosity · terminal velocity

A small metal ball is dropped into a tall jar of oil. How does its speed change with time?

Speed rises, but the Stokes drag 6πηav grows with it. When drag + buoyancy = weight, acceleration is zero: vₜ = 2a²(ρ − σ)g / 9η.

vₜ ∝ a²: bigger drops fall faster; more viscous oil → slower.

cards.term: Why do raindrops not hit us at bullet speeds?
cards.definition: Air drag grows with speed; they reach a small terminal velocity

cards.term: Example 9.9: copper ball (radius 2.0 mm) reaches 6.5 cm/s in oil (1.5 × 10³ kg/m³). η of oil?
cards.definition: ≈ 0.99 Pa s

cards.term: Correction: NCERT 9.5.1 says "refer back to Example 6.2". Which example?
cards.definition: The raindrop example is Example 5.2 (Work, Energy and Power)

cards.term: Exercise 9.13: glycerine through a 1.5 m tube (r = 1.0 cm), 4.0 × 10⁻³ kg/s. Pressure difference?
cards.definition: ≈ 9.8 × 10² Pa (Poiseuille; Reynolds number ≈ 0.3, so laminar)

cards.term: Why do surface molecules have extra energy?
cards.definition: They have neighbours on only one side, so less (negative) binding energy — about half that of a molecule inside

cards.term: Why does a liquid tend to minimise its surface area?
cards.definition: Creating surface costs energy; the liquid takes the least area that conditions allow

cards.term: Define surface tension (two ways).
cards.definition: Force per unit length in the surface, or surface energy per unit area; unit N/m = J/m²

cards.term: A film on a wire frame with a slider of length l needs force F. Surface tension?
cards.definition: \[S = \dfrac{F}{2l}\]the film has two surfaces

cards.term: Effect of temperature on surface tension?
cards.definition: Usually decreases as temperature rises

cards.term: Surface tension of water and mercury at 20 °C?
cards.definition: Water 0.0727 N/m; mercury 0.4355 N/m

cards.term: How can surface tension be measured with a balance?
cards.definition: Raise a liquid to touch a glass plate hung from the balance; extra weight to free it:\[S = \dfrac{mg}{2l}\]

cards.term: Is surface tension a property of one liquid alone?
cards.definition: No: it belongs to the interface between two substances, at least one a fluid

cards.term: Exercise 9.2(c): why is surface tension independent of surface area?
cards.definition: It is energy per unit area (or force per unit length) — a property of the interface, not of its size

cards.term: Exercise 9.17: a soap film on a 30 cm slider supports 1.5 × 10⁻² N. Surface tension?
cards.definition: S = F/2l = 2.5 × 10⁻² N/m

cards.term: Exercise 9.18: a film supports 4.5 × 10⁻² N in (a). In the other frames with the same slider length?
cards.definition: The same 4.5 × 10⁻² N: the force depends only on the length of the slider

cards.term: Define angle of contact.
cards.definition: Angle between the tangent to the liquid surface at the point of contact and the solid surface, measured inside the liquid

cards.term: Equilibrium of interfacial tensions at the contact line?
cards.definition: \[S_{la}\cos\theta + S_{sl} = S_{sa}\]

cards.term: Acute vs obtuse angle of contact: wetting?
cards.definition: Acute (water on glass, kerosene on anything): liquid wets and spreads. Obtuse (water on lotus leaf, mercury on glass): forms drops

cards.term: Why is mercury’s contact angle with glass obtuse?
cards.definition: Mercury molecules attract each other more strongly than they attract glass

cards.term: Why do detergents help cleaning, and waterproofing agents do the opposite?
cards.definition: Detergents make the contact angle small (penetrate fibres); waterproofing makes it large

cards.term: Why are free drops and bubbles spherical?
cards.definition: For a given volume a sphere has the least surface area (least surface energy)

cards.term: Excess pressure in drops and bubbles
cards.definition: Liquid drop (one surface): 2S / r; Air bubble in a liquid (one surface): 2S / r; Soap bubble in air (two surfaces): 4S / r

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
9.6.4 · excess pressure inside

Pᵢ − P₀ = ?

Liquid drop (one surface)?
Air bubble in a liquid (one surface)?
Soap bubble in air (two surfaces)?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
9.6.4 · excess pressure inside

Pᵢ − P₀ = ?

Liquid drop (one surface)2S / r
Air bubble in a liquid (one surface)2S / r
Soap bubble in air (two surfaces)4S / r

The concave side is always at higher pressure.

cards.term: Identify: which of (a), (b), (c) is a drop, a cavity (air bubble in liquid) and a soap bubble?
cards.definition:
(a) drop
(b) cavity: 2S/r
(c) soap bubble with two surfaces: 4S/r

cards.term: Example 9.10: capillary (diameter 2.00 mm) 8.00 cm under water; pressure to blow a hemispherical bubble at its end?
cards.definition: P₀ = 1.01784 × 10⁵ Pa; excess 2S/r = 146 Pa → 1.02 × 10⁵ Pa

cards.term: Exercise 9.19: mercury drop, r = 3.00 mm, S = 0.465 N/m. Excess pressure?
cards.definition: 2S/r = 310 Pa

cards.term: Exercise 9.20: soap bubble, r = 5.00 mm, S = 2.50 × 10⁻² N/m. Excess pressure?
cards.definition: 4S/r = 20 Pa

cards.term: Height of capillary rise?
cards.definition: \[h = \dfrac{2S\cos\theta}{\rho g a}\](a = tube radius)

cards.term: Why does water rise in a capillary tube?
cards.definition: The meniscus is concave, so the pressure just under it is below atmospheric; water rises until ρgh makes up the difference

cards.term: Capillary rise of water in a tube of radius 0.05 cm?
cards.definition: ≈ 2.98 cm — larger for thinner tubes (h ∝ 1/a)

cards.term: What happens to mercury in a glass capillary?
cards.definition: It is depressed below the outside level (θ obtuse, cos θ < 0)

cards.term: Everyday examples of capillarity?
cards.definition: Oil rising up a lamp wick, sap and water rising in plants, paint-brush hairs forming a tip when wet

cards.term: Teacher addition: Archimedes’ principle?
cards.definition: A body in a fluid feels an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of fluid displaced: F = σVg

cards.term: Teacher addition: fraction of a floating body that is submerged?
cards.definition: \[\dfrac{V_{in}}{V} = \dfrac{\rho_{body}}{\rho_{fluid}}\](ice in water: about 90 %)

cards.term: Fluid facts (Exercise 9.3)
cards.definition: Surface tension with temperature: decreases; Viscosity of gases with temperature: increases; Viscosity of liquids with temperature: decreases; Speed-up at a constriction follows: conservation of mass; Turbulence speed for a wind-tunnel model vs real plane: greater
